subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: choosing one course and finishing it [Action]
passage: Neel had six browser tabs of coding courses open, each promising to make him a programmer in thirty days. On Sunday he closed five, bookmarked one beginner Python course and stuck a note above his desk: One lesson a day. No new course until this one ends. His sister Nikita teased him when he refused to open a trending video about a shiny new language. Neel typed every example himself, then changed a number to see what would happen. Twenty-eight days later he finished the last lesson and wrote a tiny program of his own that counted the days to Nikita's birthday and printed a message. It was off by one on the first run. He fixed it without help and grinned at the screen.

qa.q: What did Neel write on the note above his desk?
qa.a: One lesson a day, and no new course until this one ends.

qa.q: How might Neel have felt when he refused the trending video?
qa.a: Tempted but determined: he held to his rule even though a new course looked exciting.

qa.q: What else could Neel do to make his practice stick, and why?
qa.a: Change each example and predict the result before running it, since testing his own guesses builds skill beyond copying.

qa.q: How does Neel's plan look to Nikita?
qa.a: Nikita sees her brother ignore the trend and stick with one course; she teases him, but may be impressed when he finishes and builds something for her.

grounding: A student picks one beginner course, sets one lesson a day, resists other courses and writes a small program of his own.
